title: Logical Reasoning: Simple Statements and Truth Values
summary: What a statement (proposition) is, what is not a statement, truth values, and how to tell the difference.

p: Mathematics is about careful thinking and proof. Logic decides whether an argument is valid. It is also the base of computer programming (if-else rules), law, science (testing a hypothesis) and everyday decisions such as 'if it rains, I will take an umbrella'.

A simple statement (or proposition) is a sentence that declares a fact and can be clearly called either true (T) or false (F), but not both and not neither. We use small letters p, q, r and s to stand for statements.
A false statement is still a statement, because it has a definite truth value (false).

p: A question (What is your name?) asks and does not declare. A command (Pass the salt.) tells someone to act. An opinion (This food is delicious.) is a personal feeling and cannot be checked. An exclamation (Wow, amazing!) expresses emotion. An open sentence (x + 3 = 8 or x > 10) has a letter in it, so it is true or false only when we know x.

Which are simple statements? (a) The year 2024 is a leap year. Yes, true (2024 ÷ 4 = 506 with no remainder). (b) Solve the equation. No, a command. (c) Red is a beautiful colour. No, an opinion. (d) 5 − 1 = 3. Yes, false (5 − 1 = 4). (e) x > 10. No, an open sentence.

More: The square root of 16 is 4 (true statement). Water boils at 100 °C at sea level (true statement). Please solve this problem (command). That movie was boring (opinion). 'This sentence is false' is a paradox: if it is true then it is false, and if it is false then it is true, so it has no consistent truth value and is not a simple statement.
True: Nigeria gained independence in 1960. The sum of the angles in a triangle is 180°. Water freezes at 0 °C at standard pressure. Paris is in France. 7 × 8 = 56.
False: There are 8 days in a week. Humans can breathe underwater. 5 × 6 = 31. Rome is in Asia. 9 − 4 = 6.

title: Logical Reasoning: Negation
summary: The negation of a statement, the symbol ~, how to form correct negations, the truth table of negation, and common mistakes (such as 'all' and 'some').

p: The negation of a statement says the opposite: it denies the original. The symbol is ~ and ~p is read 'not p'. Example: p: It is raining. ~p: It is not raining. p: 2 + 2 = 4. ~p: 2 + 2 ≠ 4.
Method 1: say 'It is not the case that...'. p: Monday is the first day of the week. ~p: It is not the case that Monday is the first day of the week.
Method 2: put 'not' in the right place. p: Monday is the first day of the week. ~p: Monday is not the first day of the week.
Method 3: reverse the maths symbol. > becomes ≤. < becomes ≥. = becomes ≠. For example, p: x > 5 gives ~p: x ≤ 5. And r: 10 ≥ 7 gives ~r: 10 < 7.
If the statement already has 'not', take it away: q: A triangle does not have 4 sides. ~q: A triangle has 4 sides.
Negation always flips the truth value: if p is true then ~p is false, and if p is false then ~p is true.

head: p
~p
Example
rows: p: It is raining (true). ~p: It is not raining (false).

sections.h: A tricky one: all and some
p: The negation of 'All cats are black' is NOT 'No cats are black'. It is 'Not all cats are black', or 'Some cats are not black'. If 'All cats are black' is false, it does not mean that no cat is black; it only means at least one cat is not black.
Example: let p: A square has four equal sides (true), and q: 2 is an odd number (false). Then ~p: A square does not have four equal sides (false), and ~q: 2 is not an odd number (true).

sections.h: Common mistakes and fallacies in thinking
p: Do not confuse an opinion with a statement: ask 'can it be checked as true or false?'. Make sure the negation completely reverses the meaning. Do not treat an open sentence as a statement.

Some wrong arguments (fallacies) in everyday life: attacking the person instead of the idea (Your idea is wrong because you are young); assuming one thing caused another (I wore red and won, so red is lucky); jumping to a conclusion from too little evidence (I met one rude person from that city, so everyone there is rude); using feelings instead of reasons.

activity: Write the negation of: (a) All birds can fly. (b) A rhombus is not a square. (c) 12 is a multiple of 5. (d) x < 5. (Answers: some birds cannot fly; a rhombus is a square; 12 is not a multiple of 5; x ≥ 5.)

title: Compound Statements: AND and OR
summary: Joining simple statements, the symbols for AND (conjunction) and OR (disjunction), their truth tables and examples, and how to translate sentences into symbols.

p: A compound statement joins two or more simple statements with a connective such as AND, OR or IF-THEN. Compound statements let us describe real situations: 'If it is raining, then I will take an umbrella'. The symbols are ∧ (and), ∨ (or), → (if...then), ↔ (if and only if) and ~ (not).
p ∧ q is read 'p and q'. It is true only when both p and q are true. Think of it as a demanding teacher: both must be correct.

b: p: You have a ticket (true). q: The show is today (true).
p ∧ q: You have a ticket and the show is today. This is true.
If either one is false, the whole statement is false.

p: p ∨ q is read 'p or q'. It is false only when both p and q are false. This is the inclusive OR: one, or the other, or both.

b: p: I will have tea. q: I will have coffee.
p ∨ q: I will have tea or coffee. It is true if I have either, or both. It is false only if I have neither.

p: Let p: The food is hot. Let q: The drink is cold.
The food is hot and the drink is cold: p ∧ q.
The food is not hot or the drink is cold: ~p ∨ q.
If the food is hot, then the drink is not cold: p → ~q.
Let p: It is sunny. Let q: It is hot. 'It is not sunny and it is hot' is ~p ∧ q.

title: Compound Statements: IF-THEN, IF AND ONLY IF and Truth Tables
summary: The conditional and biconditional, how to build truth tables, tautologies and contradictions, and uses in computing.

sections.h: The conditional: IF p THEN q (p → q)
p: p is the antecedent (the condition) and q is the consequent (the result). p → q is false only when p is true and q is false (a broken promise). In all other cases it is true.

Example: p: It is raining. q: The ground is wet. p → q: If it is raining, then the ground is wet. It is false only when it is raining and the ground is dry. If it is not raining, the promise is not tested, so the statement counts as true by convention.

sections.h: The biconditional: p IF AND ONLY IF q (p ↔ q)
p: p ↔ q is true when p and q have the same truth value, and false when they are different. It means (p → q) and (q → p) both hold.
Example: A figure is a square if and only if it has four equal sides and four right angles. Both parts describe exactly the same thing.
AND: true only with T, T. OR: false only with F, F. IF-THEN: false only with T then F. IF AND ONLY IF: true only when the values match.

sections.h: How to build a truth table
p: List all the combinations of T and F for the letters. Work out the inner parts first and then work outwards. Example: p ∧ ~q. Columns: p, q, ~q, p ∧ ~q. Rows: TT gives F, F, so p ∧ ~q is F. TF gives T, so T. FT gives F. FF gives F. So p ∧ ~q is true only when p is true and q is false.
Example: p ∨ ~q. TT: ~q = F, so T. TF: ~q = T, so T. FT: ~q = F, so F. FF: ~q = T, so T.
Example: (p ∨ q) → p. TT gives T. TF gives T. FT: p ∨ q = T, p = F, so F. FF: p ∨ q = F, so T.
A tautology is always true whatever the truth values: p ∨ ~p (it is raining or it is not raining). A contradiction is always false: p ∧ ~p (it is raining and it is not raining).
Evaluating: if p is T and q is T, then p → ~q is T → F, which is F. If p is F and q is F, then p ↔ q is T. If p: Lagos is in Ghana (F) and q: 2 × 3 = 6 (T), then p → q is F → T = T.

Computer programs use these ideas all the time. IF (age >= 18) AND (has_id = True) THEN grant access, ELSE refuse. A contract might say IF (contract signed) AND (payment made) THEN the obligation is met. In science, IF the hypothesis is true THEN we expect a result; if the result does not happen, the hypothesis is false.

title: Revision of First Term Mathematics
summary: A topic-by-topic revision guide for First Term: key formulas, a three-level revision method, a self-check for each topic, and exam tips.

p: Week 1 number bases, Week 2 modular arithmetic, Week 3 indices, Week 4 logarithms, Week 6 calculations with logarithms, Week 8 changing the subject and variation, Week 9 quadratic equations by factorising, Week 10 quadratic roots and graphs, Weeks 11 and 12 logical reasoning. Mathematics builds step by step, and each topic supports the next.

Level 1, understanding the why: definitions, meanings and why a formula works. Level 2, doing the how: methods and steps. Level 3, knowing the when: which method to use for which kind of question. Spend time on all three levels. Do many past WAEC and NECO questions.
Number bases: to base 10, expand with place values. From base 10, repeated division (whole part) and repeated multiplication (fraction). Carry and borrow the base.
Modular arithmetic: a ≡ b (mod m) if m divides a − b. Reduce first, then calculate. Add m to a negative result.
Indices: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ, a⁰ = 1, a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, a^(1/n) = the nth root. Equal bases, equal indices.
Logarithms: y = aˣ means x = logₐ y. log(MN) = log M + log N, log(M/N) = log M − log N, log Mᵖ = p log M. Keep the mantissa positive.
Formulas and variation: do the same to both sides; unwrap using reverse BODMAS. y = kx, y = k/x, y = kxz.
Quadratics: factorise, then use the zero product rule. Roots give x² − (sum)x + (product) = 0. A graph shows roots, vertex and axis of symmetry.
Logic: statements are true or false. ~p flips the truth value. p ∧ q needs both true. p ∨ q needs one. p → q fails only on T then F. p ↔ q needs matching values.

sections.h: A quick self-check (try each without notes)
p: Convert 1101₂ to base 10 (13). Evaluate −20 (mod 6) (4). Write 0.00032 in standard form (3.2 × 10⁻⁴). Solve 4^(x+1) = 8 (x = 1/2). Write 2⁵ = 32 in log form (log₂ 32 = 5). Make C the subject of F = (9/5)C + 32 (C = 5(F − 32)/9). If y ∝ 1/x and y = 5 when x = 4, find y when x = 10 (2). Factorise x² + 2x − 15 ((x + 5)(x − 3)). Find the equation with roots 5 and 2 (x² − 7x + 10 = 0). Write the negation of 'x < 5' (x ≥ 5).

Read each question twice. Show every step, because marks are given for method. Write units where needed. Check your answers by substituting back. Manage your time: do the easy questions first. Stay calm; you have prepared well.
